title: Simple Media System for PlayStation 2
text: Simple Media System (SMS) for PlayStation 2: exact supported video/audio formats, source-enforced playback limits, hardware-tested profiles, storage devices, setup and troubleshooting for v3.0.0-rev1.

title: What this build adds on top of SMS

title: Getting Started
text: Learn the SMS interface and play your first file end to end — the three screen areas, the pad controls, and a step-by-step first playback from a USB stick.

title: The SMS screen
text: The SMS browser is split into three stacked areas, each drawn inside its own rounded rectangle. Whichever area you are currently working in is highlighted. Learn these three and the whole interface makes sense.

title: 1 · Device menu — top row
text: A horizontal row of device icons across the top: one icon for each storage source SMS has detected (USB, MX4SIO, the internal HDD, MMCE, a network share, a CD/DVD, and so on). This is where you choose which device to browse.

title: 2 · File list — middle
text: The file browser for the device you picked: the folders and playable files on it. Directories, files and device roots use different icons so you can tell them apart at a glance. This is where you find and open your media.

title: 3 · Status line — bottom
text: A thin bar at the bottom. The current path (where you are in the filesystem) is shown on the left, and a clock sits on the right. Watch the path here to keep track of how deep into a folder tree you have gone. ℹ How SMS browses SMS reads the raw filesystem of a device and plays media wherever it happens to sit. There is no mandatory folder layout to follow and nothing special to name your files — drop a .avi or .mp3 anywhere on the stick and SMS will list it. Only supported media files (and folders) are shown in the browser.

title: Navigating with the pad
text: Everything in the browser is done with the controller. The table below covers the buttons you need. The device menu and the file list each respond a little differently, so both are noted. Button In the device menu In the file list Left / Right Move between device icons Jump back up to the device menu Down Enter the file list of the selected device Move down one item Up — Move up one item Cross ✕ Select the highlighted device and load its file list Open the selected folder, or play the selected file Triangle △ — Go up one level (folder → parent → back to the device list) L1 / L2 — Page-scroll a long list up / down Select + Circle ○ Power the PS2 off from the browser In short: Left/Right picks

title: Play your first file
text: The quickest path to a working playback is a USB stick, because almost every PS2 has a front USB port and nothing needs configuring first. Here it is end to end.

title: 1 · Format the stick
text: Format a USB flash drive as FAT32 or exFAT on your computer. Either works.

title: 2 · Copy media onto it
text: Copy a supported file to the stick — a .avi (DivX / Xvid / MPEG-4 Part 2), .mp4 ( mp4v , not H.264/H.265), .mpg video, or an .mp3 song is a safe first test. You can put it in any folder, or just at the top level. See Video Playback and Audio & Playlists for the full format lists.

title: 3 · Plug in and boot SMS
text: Insert the stick into the PS2's USB port and launch SMS.

title: 4 · Enable USB
text: On a clean install SMS does not auto-start any device — you turn on what you need. Open the settings menu and either turn on Autostart USB (so USB starts every boot from now on) or use the Start USB now item to bring it up immediately without rebooting. A USB device icon then appears in the device menu. See USB and the Settings Reference for more.

title: 5 · Pick USB in the device menu
text: Use Left/Right along the top row to highlight the USB device (it appears as a massN: device — mass0: if it's the only mass-storage device connected), press Cross to select it, then Down to enter its file list.

title: 6 · Browse to your file
text: Use Up/Down (and L1/L2 to page through a long list) to move through the files and folders. Press Cross to open a folder; press Triangle to go back up if you take a wrong turn. The status line at the bottom shows where you are.

title: 7 · Press Cross to play
text: Highlight your file and press Cross . SMS loads it and playback begins. That's it — you're watching a movie (or listening to music) on a stock PS2. ⚠ Nothing shows up in the list? If the file list is empty after entering the device, the file may not be in a format SMS recognises, or USB may not have started. Double-check the device icon is present in the top row, and confirm the file's extension is one SMS supports. The Troubleshooting page walks through the common causes.

title: Playback controls
text: Once a file is playing, a small set of buttons controls it. These are the essentials to remember: Button During playback Select Pause Start Resume Triangle △ Stop and return to the file browser So: Select to pause, Start to carry on, and Triangle to stop and go back to browsing. Video playback has more on offer — seeking, subtitles, aspect-ratio modes and an in-player menu — which are covered on the Video Playback and Subtitles pages.

title: Powering off
text: When you're done, you can turn the console off straight from SMS. In the file browser, press Select + Circle together and the PS2 powers down. You don't need to exit to the PS2 browser first.

title: Install & First Boot
text: How to get the SMS ELF onto your PlayStation 2 and run it — what you need, common launch methods (FreeMcBoot, wLaunchELF, other loaders), what the first-boot desktop looks like, and how to prepare a media device.

title: What you need
text: SMS is homebrew: it is an unsigned program, so your console needs to be able to run unsigned programs. It does not modify your PS2, install anything to the system, or require a modchip — it just needs a way in. A PS2 that can run homebrew. Any of the usual routes works — a softmod such as FreeMcBoot on a memory card, FreeDVDBoot from a burned disc, or any other exploit/loader that lets you launch an ELF. If you already run homebrew on your PS2, you are ready. The SMS build — the SMS.elf file itself. See Getting SMS below. A media device to play from. The simplest is a FAT32 or exFAT USB flash drive ; if you want to use MX4SIO, the internal HDD, i.LINK, MMCE, SMB or UDPFS instead, each is cov

title: Getting SMS
text: You need one file: the compiled SMS.elf . Grab it from the project's builds — the Releases & Changelog page tracks the available downloads. If you would rather build the ELF yourself from the source tree, the Building from Source page walks through the Docker toolchain and make . The IOP driver modules SMS needs (USB, MX4SIO, HDD, MMCE, network and the rest) are embedded inside the ELF , so a single file is genuinely all you copy — there are no loose .irx files to place beside it. ℹ One file, many names You can rename the ELF to suit your loader (some setups expect BOOT.ELF on a memory card, for example). The program is the same regardless of the filename.

title: Running the ELF
text: SMS launches like any other PS2 homebrew ELF. Use whichever method your console is already set up for — the following are the common ones, not an exhaustive list. If your loader can point at an ELF, it can launch SMS.

title: From a memory card via FreeMcBoot / OSDSYS
text: If your memory card runs FreeMcBoot , copy SMS.elf to the card (via a memory-card manager on the PS2, or an FTP/USB transfer tool) and add it to your FreeMcBoot / OSDSYS launch menu, or drop it where your menu already looks for ELFs. Then pick it from the boot menu at power-on. This is the most convenient setup — SMS is available every time you turn the console on, no disc required.

title: With wLaunchELF (uLaunchELF) off USB or a memory card
text: wLaunchELF (uLaunchELF / uLE) is the community file-manager-and-launcher most homebrew users already have. Copy SMS.elf to a USB drive or memory card, open uLaunchELF, browse to the file ( mass: for USB, mc0: / mc1: for a memory card) and press the launch/confirm button on it. uLaunchELF loads the ELF and SMS starts. There are legacy walk-through screenshots of this flow in the project's image set.

title: Launched by another loader or as an auto-boot ELF
text: Any launcher that can run an arbitrary ELF can start SMS — some people wire it into their boot menu so it runs automatically, or launch it from another homebrew front-end. As long as the loader hands control to SMS.elf , SMS behaves the same. Where SMS then saves its settings depends on where it was booted from — see Next steps .

title: From a burned disc (older consoles)
text: On consoles set up for it, SMS can also be run from optical media (for example via FreeDVDBoot or a boot disc), which is handy on an early PS2 with no other storage. Preparing a bootable disc is a console-specific process; once it boots, the SMS experience is identical. ℹ Legacy install screenshots The project keeps older step-by-step images (uLaunchELF, CD burning, FTP transfer) under docs/images/ — files named installation-*.png . They predate this fork's UI refresh but still illustrate the general launch-from-USB and copy-to-card flows.

title: First boot — what you see
text: When SMS starts you land on its desktop : a full-screen background with three bordered areas. The DEVICE menu across the top — a row of device icons (USB, MX4SIO, HDD, MMCE, network and so on). The FILE menu in the middle — the file browser / list for whatever device is selected. The STATUS line along the bottom — the current path on the left and a clock on the right. The active area is highlighted; each area sits inside its own rounded rectangle. You move between the device row and the file list with the D-pad — full navigation is covered in Getting Started and the Devices Overview . ⚠ On a clean install, nothing auto-starts Out of the box SMS starts with no storage devices running — the de

title: Preparing a media device
text: SMS is a media player that browses the raw filesystem of whatever device you point it at and plays media files wherever they sit. There is no required folder structure — no special "movies" or "cover-art" tree to build. You just put files on a drive and browse to them.

title: Format the drive FAT32 or exFAT
text: A standard FAT32 or exFAT USB flash drive or microSD works. Format it on your PC the normal way; no special partitioning is needed for USB or MX4SIO. (The internal APA HDD is the exception — that path uses the PS2's own partition scheme; see Internal HDD .)

title: Copy your media anywhere on it
text: Drop your videos, music and pictures onto the drive in whatever folders you like. SMS recognises files by extension — AVI/DivX/Xvid, mp4v MP4 and MPG/MPEG for video; MP2/MP3, AAC, AC3, FLAC, OGG and WMA for audio; JPEG for pictures; plus M3U playlists and external SRT/SUB subtitles. The full list is on the Video and Audio pages.

title: Plug it in and start the device in SMS
text: Connect the drive, then start the matching device from the SMS device menu or its Autostart toggle. Your files appear in the browser, ready to open with Cross . That is it — no import step, no database. ℹ Device names you'll see BDM mass-storage devices (USB, MX4SIO, exFAT HDD, i.LINK) all appear as massN: where N is 0, 1, 2… MMCE units show as mmce0: / mmce1: , the internal APA HDD as hdd0: , UDPFS as udpfs: , and optical discs via cdfs . You rarely need to type these — you pick devices by their icon — but they show up in the status line's path.

title: Playing a video
text: Opening a movie is a three-key affair: pick the device, walk into the folder, press play.

title: Pick the device
text: SMS opens on the device menu — the top row of device icons. Use Left / Right to highlight the device your movie lives on (a massN: device for USB / MX4SIO / HDD-exFAT / i.LINK, an mmce0: card, the internal hdd0: , a CD/DVD, smb: or udpfs: ). If the device you want is not listed, it may not be started yet — see Devices Overview for the Autostart toggles and the "Start <device> now" option.

title: Enter the file list
text: Press Down to drop into the file menu (the middle browser). Move with Up / Down , page through long folders with L1 / L2 , open a folder with ✕ , and step back up one level with △ (folder → parent → device menu). The status line at the bottom shows the current path on the left and a clock on the right.

title: Press play
text: Highlight the video file and press ✕ . SMS reads the file straight from the device and starts playback. When the movie ends — or when you stop it — you land back in the browser exactly where you were. ℹ Playing from MX4SIO This fork's headline feature is smooth video playback from an MX4SIO microSD adapter, which earlier SMS builds could not do reliably. It works exactly like any other device: pick the MX4SIO device, browse to your movie, press ✕ . See the MX4SIO page for setup.

title: Player controls
text: While a video is playing, the pad drives the player directly: Button Action Select Pause. Press it again — or Start — to resume. Start Resume from pause; during normal playback it opens the in-player menu. △ Triangle Stop playback and return to the file browser Left / Right Seek backward / forward Up / Down Volume up / down ✕ Cross Show or hide the on-screen time display □ Square Cycle the aspect / pan&scan mode — eight in all. The chosen mode is remembered in your settings. L1 / R1 Pan the picture left / right (useful once you have zoomed with Square) L1 + R1 Reset pan and zoom back to default ○ Circle Cycle the sync adjusters: A/V sync → subtitle sync (only when a subtitle is loaded) → off

title: How SMS decodes video
text: SMS earns its "good video on a stock PS2" reputation by splitting the work between the Emotion Engine and a dedicated piece of PS2 hardware — the IPU (Image Processing Unit). Decoders derived from FFmpeg. SMS's video and audio decoders started life as parts of the FFmpeg project and were then heavily reworked for the PS2 — moving to a packed image format so the decoder produces macroblocks in the IPU's native layout, and making aggressive use of the scratchpad and DMA. The original author measured roughly a 300% speed-up in video decoding versus stock FFmpeg from these changes. The IPU does the colour conversion. title: Limitations
text: SMS is a stock-console player, and a few historic limits come with that. Knowing them up front saves a lot of "why won't this play" head-scratching. Codec support is deliberately narrow. There are no H.264, H.265, VP9, AV1 or WMV video decoders. Interlaced is supported, but not part of the current fixture baseline. The MPEG-4 decoder contains interlaced field/DCT paths, and MPEG-2 supports frame- and field-encoded interlaced video. The published test profiles above are progressive. The source ceiling and the real-time ceiling are different. title: Playing audio
text: Playing a song is exactly like opening any other file — browse to it and press Cross.

title: Pick the device

title: Press Cross to play
text: Highlight the audio file and press ✕ . SMS opens the audio player and starts playback.

title: The audio player screen
text: While a track plays, SMS shows its audio player rather than a video picture. From here the pad controls playback (see Controls below). When one track finishes, SMS moves on to the next entry if there is a queue — either the rest of an M3U playlist or the other music in the same folder — otherwise playback ends and you return to the browser. Can SMS play every song in a folder automatically? Yes. SMS has long had a "play all the music in this folder" behaviour, so once one track finishes it can roll on to the next file in the same directory rather than stopping after a single song. title: Playlists (M3U)
text: An M3U file ( .m3u ) is a plain-text list of tracks to play, in order. Instead of opening songs one at a time, you open the .m3u and SMS queues every track it lists and plays them back to back. SMS treats .m3u as a first-class media file: it appears in the browser like any other, and pressing ✕ on it starts the whole list.

title: What goes in an .m3u file
text: An M3U is just one file path per line. SMS understands both the bare form (one path per line) and the extended #EXTM3U / #EXTINF form that carries a duration and a display title for each entry. A minimal example: #EXTM3U #EXTINF:213,Opening Track Music/track01.mp3 #EXTINF:187,Second Track Music/track02.flac Music/track03.ogg A few practical notes on how SMS reads them: Relative paths work — a path is taken relative to the folder the playlist lives in, so keeping the .m3u alongside its tracks is the simplest layout. title: Controls during playback
text: Audio uses the same transport controls as video, so if you already know one you know the other: Button Action Select Pause Start Resume △ Triangle Stop and return to the file browser Up / Down Volume up / down Left / Right Seek backward / forward within the track Stopping a playlist with Triangle drops you back to the browser; there is no need to let the whole queue finish.

title: Audio inside video
text: The same decoders power the soundtrack of a movie. When you play an AVI, MP4 or MPEG file, SMS decodes its embedded audio stream — commonly MP3, MP2, AAC or AC3 — right alongside the picture. If the video codec itself is unsupported (for example H.264 or H.265) the supported audio track may still play by itself. So "audio format support" and "a video's soundtrack" are two sides of the same engine; for the video side of things, see Video Playback .

title: Tips
text: Name files clearly. The browser shows filenames, so descriptive names ( 01 - Artist - Title.mp3 ) make navigating an album far easier than cryptic ones. Keep a playlist with its tracks. Because relative paths are resolved against the playlist's own folder, storing the .m3u in the same directory as the songs is the most portable arrangement — copy the folder to another device and it still works. Use the right extension. Since SMS selects the decoder by extension, an honest extension is the single most reliable way to make sure a track opens on the first try. title: Pictures
text: View JPEG photos on your PS2 with SMS — browse to a .jpg and press Cross, then step through images, rotate, and switch between fit-to-screen and actual size.

title: Overview
text: Alongside video and audio, SMS reads JPEG still images. It decodes them using the PlayStation 2's graphics hardware, so even large photos come up quickly on a stock console. The viewer works the same way no matter where the file lives — a burned disc, USB stick, MX4SIO microSD, the internal HDD, i.LINK, MMCE, an SMB share or the UDPFS network drive. If you can browse to the file, you can view it. ℹ What SMS shows The viewer handles standard baseline JPEG photos — the everyday .jpg / .jpeg files that cameras and phones produce. It is a picture viewer , not an editor: it opens and displays images, and lets you page through, rotate, and rescale them on screen.

You can still step to the next picture with Right .

title: Supported subtitle formats
text: SMS recognises three file extensions for subtitles and reads two underlying text formats: Extension Format SMS reads it as Timing style .srt SubRip (SRT) Real time, HH:MM:SS,mmm --> HH:MM:SS,mmm .sub MicroDVD / time-code "SUB" Frame-based {start}{end} , or time [start][end] / H:M:S: .txt Same reader as .sub Frame- or time-based, as above In practice, SRT is the format to prefer : it is the most common subtitle format, it is easy to find and edit, and its cues carry exact times rather than frame counts, so they line up regardless of the video's frame rate. Use a .sub / .txt file when that is what you already have. 📄 SRT example SubRip time-coded cues 📄 SUB example Frame / time-code lines

title: SubRip (.srt)
text: An SRT file is a numbered list of cues. Each cue is a sequence number, a start-and-end time line using --> , and one or more lines of text, followed by a blank line: 1 00:00:12,000 --> 00:00:15,500 This is the first subtitle. 2 00:00:16,000 --> 00:00:18,200 And this one has two lines. SMS also understands simple <b> , <i> and <u> tags around a line — bold, italic and underline — and shows those lines in their own colours (see Subtitle settings below).

title: MicroDVD-style (.sub / .txt)
text: The .sub / .txt reader accepts frame-based cues where the numbers in braces are the start and end frame , with a pipe | separating lines: {300}{375}This is the first subtitle. {400}{455}And this one has|two lines. ⚠ Frame-timed SUB files depend on frame rate Because brace-style .sub cues are counted in frames, SMS converts them to real time using the video's frame rate. If your .sub was authored for a different frame rate than your video, the lines will drift out of sync as the movie plays. SRT (real-time) files do not have this problem — if timing wanders on a SUB file, look for an SRT of the same subtitles instead.

title: Adding subtitles to a video
text: SMS finds a subtitle automatically by name-matching : it takes the video's file name, drops the extension, and looks in the same folder for a file with the same base name and a .srt , .sub or .txt extension. If it finds one, it loads it when the video starts.

title: Match the file names
text: Rename the subtitle so its base name is identical to the video. For Movie.avi the subtitle should be Movie.srt (or Movie.sub / Movie.txt ). The two names must agree up to the dot; only the extension differs.

title: Put them in the same folder
text: Copy the subtitle onto the same device and into the same directory as the video, so they sit side by side in the file list. SMS looks for the sidecar file in that same folder — it does not search elsewhere.

title: Leave "Autoload subtitles" on
text: Automatic loading is controlled by the Autoload subtitles option in Settings → Player settings (press Start in the browser to open the SMS menu), which is on by default . As long as it is on and the names match, the subtitle loads with no extra steps.

title: Play the video
text: Open the video as usual. SMS shows a brief Loading subtitles progress step while it reads the file, then the text appears over the picture at the cue times. If the subtitle file has a problem, SMS reports a subtitle error with a line number instead — see Tips & troubleshooting . Soft subtitles rendered over video during playback. ℹ Picking a subtitle by hand If a subtitle is not named to match the video, SMS can still use it — but you have to ask for it. Highlight the video and press Circle instead of Cross : SMS opens a small browser so you can pick the subtitle file yourself. It is never offered automatically; opening with Cross only ever tries the name-matching above.

title: Character encoding
text: SMS reads subtitle text as either UTF-8 or a single code page: UTF-8 is detected automatically when the file begins with a UTF-8 byte-order mark. Saving your SRT as "UTF-8 with BOM" from a text editor is the most dependable way to get accented and non-Latin characters right. Files without a UTF-8 mark are interpreted through the current code page, so plain ASCII always works, and other single-byte text works when the matching code page is in use. For scripts that need a multi-byte font (for example CJK), turn on Subtitle MBCS and select an installed multi-byte font; otherwise those characters cannot be drawn. title: Timing
text: Prefer SRT for correct sync. SRT cues carry absolute times, so they line up on any video. Frame-based .sub files are tied to a frame rate and can drift if that rate does not match the movie. If lines run consistently early or late, you likely have the wrong subtitle for that particular video file. Watch for wrapping. Very long single lines are wrapped to fit the screen. If wrapping looks awkward, reducing the font width a little often lets a line fit on one row.

title: The device bar

File menu — the middle area: the file/folder browser for whichever device is selected. Status line — the bottom strip: the current path on the left and a clock on the right. You move around the device bar with Left/Right , and press Down to drop into the file list for the highlighted device; Left/Right from the top of the file list takes you back up to the bar. title: How devices are named
text: Each source mounts under a short device name, the same style of prefix PS2 homebrew uses everywhere. Knowing the name helps you read the status line and understand which device you're on. Mount name What it is mass0: , mass1: , … BDM mass storage. USB, MX4SIO microSD, ATA/exFAT internal HDD and i.LINK drives all share this one namespace. The number ( N = 0, 1, 2…) is assigned in the order the volumes are discovered, not by which kind of device it is — so mass0: might be USB on one boot and your MX4SIO card on another, depending on what started first. mmce0: , mmce1: MMCE cards. title: Autostart vs Start now
text: SMS doesn't blindly poll every bus on boot. Instead, each device has an Autostart toggle in the settings menu, and — for anything not currently running — a Start <device> now item that brings it up on demand without a reboot.

title: Autostart <device>
text: A per-device on/off toggle. When on, SMS brings that source up automatically every time it boots. There is one toggle for each optional source: Autostart USB , Autostart i.LINK , Autostart MX4SIO , Autostart MMCE , Autostart HDD (the classic APA/PFS path) and Autostart HDD BDM (the ATA/exFAT path). Networking is a single choice presented as three rows — Autostart HOST (ps2dev) , Autostart SMB and Autostart UDPFS — and picking one clears the other two.

title: Start <device> now
text: When a device is not already running, a matching "Start <device> now" item appears so you can spin it up for this session without turning on Autostart or rebooting — handy for a one-off (plug in a drive, start it, browse it).

title: Clean install = nothing runs
text: Out of the box, no source auto-starts . You decide what to enable. This keeps boot fast and avoids probing hardware you don't have. Clearing the config returns you to this state (see Where settings live ). ℹ Just want to try a device? Use Start now . It doesn't change your saved config, so the device won't come up again on the next boot unless you also flip its Autostart toggle. Once you know a source is one you use every session, turn on Autostart for it. Full details of every toggle live on the Settings Reference .

title: Mutual exclusions

Only one can be active at a time — if MX4SIO is running, starting MMCE will decline, and vice versa. title: USB
text: Play media from a USB drive on SMS — plug a FAT32 or exFAT stick into the PS2's USB port, mount it as massN: over BDM, and browse your files wherever they sit.

title: Overview
text: A USB mass-storage device — a flash drive/stick, or a self-powered USB hard disk — connects to the PS2's USB port. SMS loads its USB driver on the IOP and mounts the drive through BDM (the Block Device Manager), the same mounting layer used by MX4SIO, the exFAT internal HDD and i.LINK. Because they all share that layer, USB drives take device names in the common massN: namespace: the first mounted BDM volume is mass0: , the next mass1: , and so on. Once mounted, the drive appears as a device icon in the device menu (the top row of the SMS screen). Select it and press Down to drop into the file list and browse. SMS plays media directly off the drive — video, audio and pictures alike. ⚠ Which

title: Compatibility
text: SMS reads USB drives formatted with a standard PC filesystem and a normal partition table. Requirement Details Filesystem FAT32 or exFAT Partition table MBR (master boot record) — the usual default for USB media Device type USB flash drive / stick, or a self- or externally-powered USB hard disk Media location Anywhere on the drive — SMS browses the raw filesystem, so any folder layout works Format the drive as a single MBR partition. FAT32 is the most universally compatible choice; use exFAT if you need to store individual files larger than 4 GB (see Tips ). There is no coverart, ISO or special-folder requirement — SMS is a media player that reads your files where they are, not a game loader

title: Preparing the drive
text: Play media from a USB drive on SMS — plug a FAT32 or exFAT stick into the PS2's USB port, mount it as massN: over BDM, and browse your files wherever they sit.

title: Format as FAT32 or exFAT
text: On your PC, format the USB drive as a single FAT32 or exFAT partition on an MBR partition table. A quick full format (not just a fresh copy over old data) also gives you a clean, low-fragmentation filesystem to start from.

title: Copy your media anywhere
text: Drag your videos, music and pictures onto the drive. You can drop them at the root, or organise them into folders however you like — SMS shows whatever directory tree is on the drive. There is no mandatory folder structure: no DVD/ , CD/ or ART/ tree, no ISOs. Just files.

title: Use supported formats
text: Copy files SMS can play: video such as AVI (DivX/Xvid/MPEG-4 Part 2), MP4 (MPEG-4 Part 2 mp4v ) and MPEG program streams; audio such as MP2/MP3 , AAC , FLAC , OGG , WMA and AC3 ; and JPEG pictures. H.264/H.265 video is not supported even when stored in an MP4 file. External SRT/SUB subtitles and M3U playlists work too. The Video and Audio pages list every format in detail.

title: Eject cleanly, then plug into the PS2
text: Safely eject the drive from your PC so all writes are flushed, then plug it into the PlayStation 2's USB port. Fat consoles have their ports on the front; slims have them at the top-front. Then boot SMS.

title: Enabling USB in SMS
text: On a clean install SMS starts nothing automatically — you turn on the devices you want. There are two ways to get USB running.

title: Autostart USB (recommended)
text: In the settings menu, turn on Autostart USB . From then on, SMS loads the USB driver at boot, so a plugged-in drive is detected and mounted automatically every time you start the player. This is the set-and-forget option if you use USB regularly.

title: Start USB now (on demand)
text: If USB is not currently running — for example you left Autostart off — SMS offers a Start USB support item so you can bring the device up on the spot, without rebooting. If USB is already running and you plug a drive in afterwards, that item is gone; use Refresh connections at the bottom of Device settings instead, which re-scans the mass slots for newly attached drives. Trigger it, give the driver a moment to load and enumerate the drive, and the USB device appears in the device menu. ℹ Pick USB in the device menu Once USB is running, use Left/Right in the device menu to move the highlight onto the USB ( massN: ) device, then press Down to enter its file list. title: Browsing & playing
text: Inside the file list, navigation is the same as anywhere in SMS: Input Action Up / Down Move the selection through the file list L1 / L2 Page-scroll through a long list Cross (✕) Open the highlighted folder, or start playing the highlighted file Triangle (△) Go up one level — folder → parent → back out to the device menu Left / Right Return to the device menu to switch devices Select a video, music track or picture with Cross and it plays. During video or audio playback, Select pauses, Start resumes, and Triangle stops and returns you to the browser. Subtitles and M3U playlists that live alongside your media on the USB drive are picked up automatically — see Subtitles and Audio & Playlists .

title: Tips & troubleshooting
text: Use exFAT for files over 4 GB. FAT32 cannot hold a single file larger than 4 GB. If you have a long or high-bitrate video that exceeds that, format the drive as exFAT instead — SMS reads both. Keep files unfragmented. On a heavily-fragmented drive, playback can stutter as the PS2 chases scattered pieces of a file. The simplest fix is to copy everything off, reformat the drive, and copy it back so each file lands contiguously. On slow or old media this matters more than anything else. Avoid too many small fragments. title: MX4SIO (microSD)
text: Play video, audio and pictures from a microSD in an MX4SIO adapter — the headline feature of this SMS build: reliable MX4SIO playback over the PS2 memory-card (SIO2) bus, with its own device icon.

title: What MX4SIO is
text: An MX4SIO adapter takes a microSD card and presents it to the PS2 through the memory-card slot, communicating over the console's SIO2 controller bus (the same bus the pad and memory card use). To SMS the card looks like any other BDM (Block Device Manager) mass-storage volume: it is mounted from the FAT/exFAT layer and surfaces as massN: , exactly the abstraction USB, exFAT-over-ATA and i.LINK all share. That means SMS does not need a special "MX4SIO file browser" — it simply browses the card's raw filesystem and plays whatever media files it finds, wherever they sit. title: Why it is the headline feature
text: Plenty of PS2 tools can mount an MX4SIO card and list its directories — but that is the easy part. A media player is different: it streams large reads continuously while the rest of the console is busy decoding audio, driving the GUI and polling the pad. Under exactly those conditions, earlier attempts to use MX4SIO in SMS would mount the card and show the file list, then stall the moment you tried to actually play a file . This build fixes that. Video and audio now play smoothly from a microSD in an MX4SIO adapter — the same experience you get from USB or the internal HDD. title: Format the microSD

text: You don't need to know any of this to use MX4SIO — but in short: a continuously-streaming media player asks a lot more of an SD-over-SIO2 card than a lightweight file manager does, because it reads constantly while also decoding audio and driving the GUI. title: Internal HDD
text: Use the PS2's internal hard drive with SMS two ways — the classic APA/PFS partitions, or a plain exFAT drive read over ATA as a massN: BDM device — and how to choose between them.

title: Two ways to use the HDD
text: SMS is a media player, not a game loader — so the HDD is just another place to keep your video, music and pictures. The catch is that the internal drive can be formatted in one of two schemes, and SMS reaches each one through a different driver stack: 💽 APA / PFS The PS2's own partition scheme 🗂️ exFAT via ATA A plain drive as massN: They are mutually exclusive : both paths want to own the internal ATA bus, so whichever one starts first takes it and the other quietly steps aside. You choose which by picking the matching Autostart toggle — see Choosing one below. title: APA / PFS — the PS2's native HDD format
text: The APA partition scheme and PFS filesystem are the PS2's own native HDD formats — the same ones used by Sony's HDD-OSD (the "PlayStation BB Navigator" era) and by the classic homebrew HDD tools. On this kind of drive, SMS lists the PFS partitions it finds on the APA table as a folder-like list. Pick one with Cross to mount it and browse the media inside; SMS remembers the partition you last used and re-enters it automatically on the next boot. There is no required partition name. ℹ No special partition name needed Older guides tell you to create a partition called SMS_Media . That has not been necessary for a long time and this build does not look for it — SMS shows you every PFS partition

title: Preparing an APA drive
text: SMS doesn't format drives or create partitions itself — you do that ahead of time with the usual PS2 HDD tools (HDD-OSD, or a homebrew APA/PFS partition manager such as uLaunchELF). The short version:

title: Format the drive as APA
text: Initialise the internal drive with the standard PS2 APA scheme, the same way you would for any HDD-OSD / OPL-era setup. This is a one-time step done from a HDD tool, not from SMS.

title: Create a PFS media partition
text: Make a PFS partition to hold your media — call it whatever you like. Copy your video, audio and picture files into it (folders inside are fine — SMS browses the raw tree).

title: Enable the APA path in SMS
text: Turn on Autostart HDD APA in the settings (or use Start HDD APA now — see Enabling & tips ). SMS starts the HDD driver stack and lists the drive's PFS partitions.

title: Browse and play
text: Pick the internal-HDD icon in the device menu and press Down into the list. Choose your partition with Cross to mount it, then open any file with Cross as usual — SMS remembers the partition and re-enters it on the next boot. It behaves exactly like every other SMS source — the raw filesystem, no mandatory folder layout. ⚠ APA drives are ~2 TB and older-drive friendly The APA scheme addresses drives up to about 2 TB . If you have a larger drive — or you'd simply rather copy files from a PC without any PS2-side tools — use the exFAT route below instead.

title: exFAT via ATA
text: The modern alternative skips APA entirely. Format the internal drive as plain exFAT on your PC, drop your media anywhere on it, and let SMS read the drive through its ATA block driver . Because that driver plugs into the same Block Device Manager (BDM) that handles USB, MX4SIO and i.LINK, the internal drive simply appears as another massN: device in SMS — no PS2-specific formatting, no partition juggling. ℹ One shared massN: namespace USB, MX4SIO, the exFAT internal HDD and i.LINK all mount into the same massN: pool ( N = 0, 1, 2…). The number is assigned as devices come up, so a drive is mass0: if it mounts first, mass1: if a USB stick got there ahead of it, and so on. You browse it by pick

title: Preparing an exFAT drive
text: Use the PS2's internal hard drive with SMS two ways — the classic APA/PFS partitions, or a plain exFAT drive read over ATA as a massN: BDM device — and how to choose between them.

title: Format exFAT on your PC
text: Connect the drive to a computer (or format it in-bay with a PC-side tool) and format it as exFAT . Leave the allocation-unit / cluster size at the default for the drive's capacity rather than choosing a custom value.

title: Copy your media
text: Drag your video, audio and picture files onto the drive — into any folders you like. SMS browses the raw filesystem, so there is no required folder tree (no OPL-style DVD/ / CD/ layout).

title: Fit the drive and enable the BDM path
text: Install the drive in the console's HDD bay, then turn on Autostart HDD BDM in SMS (or Start HDD BDM now ). SMS brings up the ATA driver and the exFAT volume mounts as massN: .

title: Browse and play
text: Select the internal-HDD icon in the device menu and open files just like any other massN: device. ⚠ Copy large files one at a time The PS2 reads far better from files that aren't fragmented. When you copy a batch to an exFAT drive, add big video files individually rather than dumping the whole folder in one go — many PC copy operations interleave a large batch, fragmenting every file. Sequential copies keep playback smooth.

title: Choosing one — they're mutually exclusive
text: Here's the important constraint: the APA/PFS path and the exFAT/ATA path both own the internal ATA bus , so only one can be active at a time. SMS enforces this with a simple "first come, first served" rule — whichever backend starts first claims the bus, and the other declines to start for that session. ℹ First to start owns the bus If the APA HDD path comes up first, the exFAT/ATA path won't start (and vice versa). This isn't an error — it's SMS keeping two drivers that both drive the same internal disk from stepping on each other. To switch schemes, disable the one you don't want (or don't autostart it) and reboot so the other can claim the bus cleanly. Practically, that means you decide u

title: Enabling & tips
text: On a clean install nothing auto-starts — you turn on exactly what you need. The relevant controls live in the settings menu: Autostart HDD APA — brings up the classic APA/PFS path at boot and lists the drive's PFS partitions. Autostart HDD BDM — brings up the exFAT drive over ATA at boot as a massN: device. Start HDD … now — when a device isn't already running, SMS also offers an on-demand start item, so you can bring the HDD up without a reboot. Handy for testing which scheme your drive actually mounts. ℹ If a start stalls, watch the status line Starting the internal HDD spins the drive up and probes it, which takes a moment. SMS shows the current stage on the status line as it goes; if a s

title: Practical tips
text: Match the toggle to the format. An exFAT drive will not mount under Autostart HDD APA, and an APA/PFS partition won't appear under Autostart HDD BDM. If a drive doesn't show up, you almost certainly enabled the wrong path for how it's formatted. Big drive? Use exFAT. APA tops out around 2 TB; exFAT lets you use larger drives and skip PS2-side tooling entirely — just format on a PC and copy files. Big library already on APA? Keep it. If your drive is already APA-formatted, the APA path reads your existing PFS partitions directly with no conversion — whatever they are named. The drive is optional hardware. title: i.LINK (IEEE 1394 / FireWire)
text: Play media in SMS from an i.LINK (IEEE 1394 / FireWire) external drive — mounted as a massN: device — including enabling it, preparing a FAT32/exFAT drive, and browsing your files.

title: What is i.LINK?
text: i.LINK is Sony's branding for the IEEE 1394 serial bus — the same standard sold elsewhere as FireWire (Apple) or Lynx (Texas Instruments). Many PS2 models expose a 4-pin i.LINK port on the front or side of the console. It was originally intended for connecting the PS2 to other PS2s and to digital video gear; in practice, on homebrew, it is a handy way to attach an external hard drive or SSD enclosure that speaks FireWire. When SMS starts its i.LINK support, it loads the IOP driver modules that walk the FireWire bus, find any attached storage, log in to it and expose its partitions to the console's block-device layer. From that point on the drive is just another BDM mass device — the same gen

title: Compatibility
text: i.LINK storage in SMS is for external FireWire drives : a hard disk or SSD in an enclosure (or a dock) that connects over IEEE 1394. The drive is read through the same filesystem layer as every other BDM mass device, so the same formatting rules apply. Property What works Connection i.LINK / IEEE 1394 / FireWire, into the PS2's i.LINK port Device type External hard drive or SSD enclosure that presents as FireWire mass storage Filesystem FAT32 or exFAT Appears as massN: (shares the BDM namespace with USB, MX4SIO and ATA/exFAT HDD) Role in SMS A browsable media source — play video, audio and pictures directly from it ℹ A modest note on tested drives i.LINK support is confirmed working on real

title: Preparing the drive
text: Set the drive up on your PC the same way you would prepare a USB drive for SMS, then copy your media onto it.

title: Format FAT32 or exFAT
text: On your computer, format the FireWire drive as FAT32 or exFAT . exFAT is the easy choice for large drives and large files; FAT32 is fine for smaller drives.

title: Copy your media on
text: Drop your video, audio and picture files onto the drive. SMS browses the raw filesystem — there is no mandatory folder layout to follow. Put your files wherever you like (a simple folder such as /Movies or /Music just keeps things tidy) and SMS will let you navigate to them.

title: Eject, connect, and power the drive
text: Safely eject the drive from your PC, then plug it into the PS2's i.LINK port with a FireWire cable. If your enclosure needs external power, make sure it is powered and the disk is spun up before (or as) SMS looks for it. ℹ Which formats will play Any file SMS understands will play from an i.LINK drive: video (DivX / XviD / MPEG-4 Part 2 AVI, mp4v MP4, MPEG-1/2 program streams), audio (MP2/MP3, AAC, AC3, FLAC, OGG Vorbis, WMA) and JPEG pictures, plus M3U playlists and external SRT / SUB subtitles. See Video Playback and Audio & Playlists for the full detail.

title: Enabling i.LINK in SMS
text: On a clean install nothing auto-starts — you turn on the devices you want. i.LINK is off until you enable it, in one of two ways.

title: Turn on Autostart i.LINK (persistent)
text: In the settings menu, enable the Autostart i.LINK toggle. From then on, every time SMS boots it will bring the FireWire bus up and look for an attached drive automatically. This is the "set it and forget it" option if you keep a drive on the i.LINK port. Your choice is saved with the rest of your settings (see Settings ).

title: Or use "Start i.LINK now" (on demand)
text: If i.LINK is not already running, a Start i.LINK now item is available so you can bring it up on the spot — no reboot needed. Handy when you only occasionally attach a FireWire drive and would rather not auto-start it every boot.

title: Give it a couple of seconds
text: FireWire discovery is not instant. After i.LINK starts, the driver needs a short moment — on the order of a couple of seconds — to discover the drive on the bus and log in to it before it appears in the device menu. If it does not show up immediately, wait a beat; this delay is normal. ⚠ Have the drive connected and ready first Because discovery happens shortly after i.LINK starts, plug the drive in and make sure it is powered and spun up before you enable Autostart i.LINK or press Start i.LINK now. A drive that is still spinning up, or connected after the scan, may be missed until the next start.

title: Browse & play
text: Once the drive is discovered it appears in the top device menu as a massN: volume. From there it behaves exactly like any other storage device in SMS:

title: Pick the device
text: In the device menu at the top, use Left / Right to highlight your i.LINK volume (a massN: entry), then press Down to drop into the file list.

title: Navigate to your file
text: In the file list, move with Up / Down , page through long lists with L1 / L2 , open a folder or start a file with Cross , and go up one level with Triangle . The bottom status line shows your current path on the left and a clock on the right.

title: Play
text: Open a video, track or picture and it plays straight from the FireWire drive. During playback, Select pauses, Start resumes, and Triangle stops and returns you to the browser. ℹ Which massN: is my i.LINK drive? USB, MX4SIO, i.LINK and exFAT/ATA HDD all share the single massN: numbering pool, and the number a device gets depends on what started and in what order. If you have several BDM devices connected at once, the simplest way to tell them apart is to open each massN: entry and recognise its contents. With only the i.LINK drive attached it will typically be mass0: .

title: Notes & good to know
text: Its own bus. i.LINK runs over the FireWire (IEEE 1394) bus, independent of USB and of the SIO2 / memory-card bus. It happily works alongside USB and MX4SIO at the same time — there is no conflict between them. Confirmed on hardware. i.LINK storage has been tested and works on a real PS2 in this fork, mounting an exFAT drive over FireWire next to the other working devices. A couple of seconds to appear. The short discovery/login delay after starting i.LINK is expected — give the bus a moment before assuming the drive is not there. FAT32 or exFAT only. Keep the drive formatted FAT32 or exFAT; other filesystems are not read. No special folder tree. SMS reads the raw filesystem and plays media w

title: MMCE (SD2PSX / MemCard PRO2)
text: Play media in SMS from an SD2PSX or MemCard PRO2 in the memory-card slot — the MMCE protocol mounts the SD card as mmce0: / mmce1:, browsed and played like any other device.

title: What is MMCE?
text: MMCE stands for Memory Card Mass-storage Emulation . Devices like the SD2PSX and the MemCard PRO2 plug into a PS2 memory-card slot and, as well as pretending to be a memory card, can present the full contents of their SD card to homebrew over a small command protocol. That protocol was designed by bbsan2k , and it is the same protocol the wider PS2 homebrew scene uses to reach these adapters. When SMS starts MMCE support, it loads the IOP driver that talks to the adapter and then checks the memory-card slots for a device that answers. Any card it finds is added to the device menu as a browsable volume: mmce0: for the first slot, mmce1: for the second. From that point on MMCE is just another

title: MMCE vs MX4SIO
text: Both MMCE adapters and MX4SIO put an SD card in the memory-card slot, so it is easy to confuse them — but they are two completely different things, driven two different ways, and they cannot run at the same time . MMCE (SD2PSX / MemCard PRO2) MX4SIO Hardware SD2PSX or MemCard PRO2 adapter MX4SIO (a.k.a. SIO2SD) microSD adapter How SMS reads it The bbsan2k MMCE protocol The MX4SIO block-device ( BDM ) driver Appears as mmce0: / mmce1: massN: (shared with USB, ATA, i.LINK) Enable with Autostart MMCE Autostart MX4SIO ⚠ Only one memory-card-slot SD device at a time MMCE and MX4SIO both use the console's SIO2 / memory-card-slot bus . title: Preparing the card
text: Getting media onto an MMCE card is the same job as preparing any SD card — do it on your PC, then load it into the adapter.

title: Format the SD card
text: Format the SD card as FAT32 or exFAT . FAT32 is the most universally compatible; exFAT is handy for very large cards and files over 4 GB. Either works with SMS.

title: Copy your media on
text: Copy your video, audio and picture files onto the card in whatever folder structure you like — SMS reads the raw filesystem, so there is no required layout. Keep any external subtitle file ( .srt / .sub ) next to its video with a matching name so SMS pairs them automatically. See Video and Audio for the exact formats SMS plays.

title: Load the card into the adapter
text: Insert the SD card into your SD2PSX or MemCard PRO2 , then seat the adapter in a PlayStation 2 memory-card slot. Slot 1 becomes mmce0: and slot 2 becomes mmce1: . ℹ Card as memory card and media source An SD2PSX or MemCard PRO2 can still act as your virtual memory card at the same time as SMS reads media from its SD card — the two roles co-exist. SMS only reads files from the card; it does not touch your saved-game memory-card images.

title: Enabling MMCE in SMS
text: On a fresh install nothing auto-starts — you switch on the devices you actually use. MMCE is controlled from the settings menu, right alongside the other per-device Autostart toggles.

title: Turn off MX4SIO first (if it is on)
text: Because MMCE and MX4SIO share the memory-card bus, make sure Autostart MX4SIO is off before you try MMCE. If MX4SIO is already running, SMS will decline to start MMCE.

title: Enable Autostart MMCE
text: Open the settings menu and switch on Autostart MMCE in the device list. With it on, SMS loads the MMCE driver and scans the memory-card slots each time it boots, mounting any card it finds.

title: Or start it on demand
text: Don't want to reboot? Start MMCE support is always listed in Device settings — choose it to load the driver and scan the slots immediately. It is deliberately shown even when MMCE is already up (harmless no-op) and even when MX4SIO holds the SIO2 bus, in which case it reports an error telling you why MMCE cannot start. — the device shows up in the device menu without a restart.

title: Save your settings
text: Let SMS save the configuration so your choice sticks on the next boot. Settings live on the memory card at mc0:/SMS/SMS.cfg ; in this fork, if SMS was booted from another device with no memory card, they save next to the SMS program on that device instead. See Settings . ⚠ MMCE will not start while MX4SIO is running This is the single most common surprise. If you turn on Autostart MMCE but nothing appears, check that Autostart MX4SIO is off. They cannot share the bus, so whichever one you leave enabled is the one you get.

title: Browsing & playing
text: Once MMCE is up, it behaves like any other device in the three-part SMS interface — a device menu across the top, the file list in the middle, and the status line (current path on the left, clock on the right) along the bottom.

title: Pick the device
text: In the device menu (top row), press Left / Right to highlight your MMCE device — the SD2PSX / MemCard PRO2 icon — then press Down to drop into its file list.

title: Navigate the card
text: In the file list, use Up / Down to move and L1 / L2 to page through long folders. Press Cross to open a folder or start a file, and Triangle to go up one level (folder → parent → back to the device menu). Left / Right returns you to the device menu.

title: Play
text: Select a video, track or picture and press Cross to play it. During playback, Select pauses, Start resumes, and Triangle stops and returns you to the browser. Subtitles, M3U playlists and everything else work exactly as they do on other devices.

title: Notes & tips
text: Slot 1 mounts as mmce0: and slot 2 mounts as mmce1: . If you have two MMCE adapters, both can appear at once — each as its own device. MMCE and MX4SIO are mutually exclusive — both use the memory-card (SIO2) bus, so enable only one. USB, the internal HDD, i.LINK and SMB are unaffected and can run alongside your MMCE card. There is no required folder layout . SMS reads the raw SD card and plays media from wherever you put it — this is a media player, not a game loader, so there are no disc images or artwork folders to set up. Format the SD card FAT32 or exFAT . Use exFAT if you need files larger than 4 GB. Keep external subtitles ( .srt / .sub ) next to the matching video so SMS pairs them au

title: SMB Network Share
text: Play media from a Windows or Samba network share over Ethernet — set up an SMB (CIFS) share, configure the server, share, and credentials on-screen in SMS, then browse and play like a local device.

title: Overview
text: An SMB (Server Message Block) share is just a folder on another computer that has been made available over the local network. Windows calls this "File Sharing"; Linux and NAS boxes usually run Samba , an open-source implementation of the same protocol. SMS includes a small SMB1/CIFS client that connects to one of these shares over the PS2's Ethernet port and lets you walk its folders exactly as if it were a local disc — pick a movie and press play, and SMS streams it over the wire. On the device menu the share shows up as a network device alongside your other sources. Once connected, navigation, playback, subtitles and playlists all behave the same as they do for a local device — the only di

title: Requirements
text: A PS2 network adapter and a wired Ethernet connection to the same LAN as your PC or NAS. SMS's network support is wired only — there is no built-in Wi-Fi. A PC, NAS, or other device on that LAN that is sharing a folder over SMB1 / CIFS . Because modern Windows and Samba ship with SMBv1 switched off, you generally have to enable the SMB1 feature on the server (or use a device/NAS that still serves it) — this is the single most common reason a share is invisible. The server's IP address on the LAN, the exact share name , and a set of credentials — a username and password, or a guest / anonymous login if the share allows it. The PS2 already on the network with an IP address (see Network Setup )

title: Setting up the share on your PC or NAS
text: This part happens on the computer, not on the PS2. The goal is a shared folder that answers to SMB1 and that you can reach with a known username and password (or as a guest). The exact steps differ by operating system, but the shape is always the same:

title: Create and share a folder
text: Make a folder to hold your media — for example a "Movies" folder — and turn on file sharing for it. On Windows this is Properties → Sharing (or "Give access to"); on a NAS it is the box's Shared Folders / SMB service; on Linux it is a Samba [share] entry. Write down the exact share name you give it — SMS needs it spelled the same way, case included.

title: Decide on access: user or guest
text: Either grant a specific username access to the share and set a password for it, or (if your OS allows it and you don't mind) enable guest / anonymous access so no password is needed. Note down whichever you choose — you'll type it into SMS.

title: Make sure SMB1 is being served
text: On a modern Windows PC, enable the "SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support" Windows feature; on a modern Samba server, allow the old protocol (an SMB1 -friendly min protocol in the Samba config). Many NAS units have a checkbox to allow SMBv1 as well. Without this step the share exists but SMS cannot speak to it.

title: Find the server's IP address
text: Note the PC / NAS IP address on your LAN (for example 192.168.1.50 ). SMS connects by IP. Give the machine a fixed / reserved address if you can, so it doesn't change between sessions.

title: Configuring the SMB share in SMS
text: Everything below is done on the console with the pad. This fork replaces the old fiddly per-character picker with a real on-screen keyboard , so you type the server address, share and credentials directly — there is no config file to prepare on a PC beforehand. You add a share once; SMS remembers it. ℹ The on-screen keyboard When you open one of the text fields, SMS pops up a full on-screen keyboard: move the D-pad to a character and press Cross to type it, use Circle to backspace and Square for a space, and commit the field with Triangle (or the OK key). It covers digits, upper- and lower-case letters and the common symbols ( . _ - / @ : and more), so full server names, usernames and passwo

title: Connecting & browsing
text: Play media from a Windows or Samba network share over Ethernet — set up an SMB (CIFS) share, configure the server, share, and credentials on-screen in SMS, then browse and play like a local device.

title: Bring up the network
text: With the network configured (and Autostart SMB on, or started on demand), SMS connects to your LAN and then to the SMB server you saved.

title: Select the network device
text: In the top row Device menu , use Left / Right to land on the network / SMB device, then press Down to drop into the file list.

title: Browse the share
text: The middle File menu now lists the contents of the share. Move with Up / Down (use L1 / L2 to page through long folders), press Cross to open a folder or start a file, and Triangle to go up one level. The current path shows in the status line at the bottom left.

title: Play
text: Pick a video, track or picture and press Cross . Playback, subtitles and playlists work just as they do from a local device — during playback Select pauses, Start resumes, and Triangle stops and returns you to the browser. ⚠ Streaming over the network Playback quality depends on your LAN and the file's bitrate. A wired connection to a modern router handles typical SMS video fine, but very high-bitrate files may benefit from copying to a local device (USB, MX4SIO, HDD) instead. If a file stutters over SMB but plays cleanly from a local source, the network is the limiting factor.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom Most likely cause & fix The share never appears / SMS can't connect at all SMBv1 is disabled on the server — the number-one cause. Enable "SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support" on Windows, allow the old protocol in Samba, or use a device that still serves SMB1. Can't reach the server, but the LAN seems fine Check the IP address you typed matches the server's current address (it may have changed if it isn't reserved). Confirm the PS2 itself has a valid IP — see Network Setup . Connects, but access is refused Wrong credentials . Re-check the username and password, and confirm that account actually has permission to the share. If you meant to use guest access, make sure the share allows it

title: Limitation: SMB1 only
text: SMS's network share support is built on the original SMB1 (CIFS) protocol. It does not speak SMB2 or SMB3 , the newer versions that modern operating systems prefer. That is why a stock, up-to-date Windows PC or NAS won't be visible until you re-enable the legacy SMB1 feature on it. Speaking the newer protocols would require a substantial rewrite of the client, so for now the rule of thumb is simple: if the server serves SMB1, SMS can use it; if it only serves SMB2/3, it can't. Why is SMB1 a security concern, and is enabling it safe? SMBv1 is an old protocol with known weaknesses, which is exactly why Microsoft and the Samba project switched it off by default. Do not expose it to the internet

title: CDDAFS — the burned-CD trick that started SMS
text: A stock PlayStation 2 refuses to boot or read a burned data CD-R — the console's copy protection treats it as an "illegal" disc. Eugene Plotnikov's answer, borrowing an idea from Drakonite's UMCDR, was CDDAFS : a way of storing ordinary data files on a disc that is physically laid out as an audio CD . Because the PS2 happily authenticates an audio-CD-shaped disc, a CDDAFS disc reads on (in Eugene's words) hopefully any PS2 — no modchip needed. This is the very first component of SMS, and the reason the project is a "system" and not just a player. ℹ What CDDAFS actually is In Eugene's own description, CDDAFS "just stores data on a CD audio disk, which can be read on any PS2." The disc's audio

title: Building a CDDAFS disc (conceptually)
text: You do not author a CDDAFS disc on the PS2 — you build it on a PC and burn it. Eugene wrote a companion Windows program, CDXplorer , whose job is to take your files and produce a cue/bin pair describing the special audio-CD-with-data layout. You then burn that cue/bin to a CD-R with a burning program, using a Disc-At-Once mode (Eugene used Nero's "Disc-At-Once / 96" option). CDXplorer can also read an existing CDDAFS disc back, so you can copy your files off again. ⚠ CDDAFS is a create-on-PC, play-on-PS2 workflow The CDDAFS filesystem is intentionally simple, and the tooling is old and Windows-only. Treat the exact cue/bin build as a PC task with CDXplorer (or a compatible CDDAFS builder), n

title: Add your files on the PC
text: In CDXplorer (or a compatible CDDAFS tool), start a new disc and add the media files you want on it — for example a DivX/XviD movie and its soundtrack. The classic use is a single feature-length movie per disc.

title: Produce the cue/bin
text: Have the tool generate the cue/bin pair that describes the CDDAFS (audio-CD) layout. This is the image you will burn — not a normal data ISO.

title: Burn to CD-R with Disc-At-Once
text: Burn the cue/bin to a blank CD-R using a Disc-At-Once write mode. Because the disc masquerades as an audio CD, the PS2 accepts it. Burn slowly and use good media (see Notes ).

title: Play it in SMS
text: Put the disc in the PS2, launch SMS, wait for the disc device to appear, drop into the file list, and open your movie. It plays straight off the burned CD-R on a stock console. How does a CDDAFS disc lay its data out? (the historical detail) From Eugene's README: track 0 is a control track holding a GUID, a disc name and description, a small disc picture, and a table of 32×32 icon images, followed by a directory table. Each remaining audio track is a directory containing file entries — a name, an icon index, and the file's start offset and size — followed by the file data itself. title: DVD-Video — playing files from a burned DVD
text: SMS can also read media files from a DVD-Video disc on an unmodified console. Support for reading .avi (and other) files from DVD-Video discs was added with a cdvd.irx driver that understands the UDF filesystem DVD-Video uses. In practice this means you can author a burned DVD in the DVD-Video layout, drop your media files into it, and browse them in SMS exactly like any other device — with the big advantage that a DVD holds far more than a CD-R, so you are not limited to a single small movie per disc. ℹ Why "DVD-Video" and not a plain data DVD The DVD-Video layout is the burned-disc form a stock PS2 is happiest reading, which is why SMS's DVD path targets it. When you make the disc on your

title: Data CD / DVD (ISO)
text: Beyond the two burned-disc tricks above, SMS also reads ordinary ISO 9660 / UDF data discs — the standard data-disc format. On consoles able to read them, an ISO data CD or DVD simply appears as a disc device you can browse, with your media files inside. This is handy when you already have media on a normal data disc, or when your setup can read data discs directly. The browsing and playback experience is identical to CDDAFS and DVD-Video once the disc is recognised — the only difference is how the disc was mastered.

title: Audio CD (CDDA)
text: SMS also plays plain Audio CDs — ordinary Red Book music CDs. Insert a music CD and SMS reads its table of contents, mounts it as an audio disc, and lists its tracks for playback. This is separate from CDDAFS: a CDDAFS disc only looks like an audio CD to sneak data past the copy protection, whereas a genuine Audio CD holds real audio tracks that SMS plays as music. ℹ Audio CD vs data disc — SMS decides for you When a disc goes in, SMS inspects it and routes it correctly on its own: a real music CD becomes an Audio CD you play track by track, while a data disc (CDDAFS, ISO, or DVD-Video) becomes a filesystem you browse. title: Burning quality & media
text: Burn slowly, on good media. A stock PS2 optical drive — especially an older or well-used one — is far happier reading a carefully burned disc. Use quality blank CD-R / DVD-R media and a conservative write speed. CDDAFS needs Disc-At-Once. Because a CDDAFS disc is written as an audio CD, burn its cue/bin with a Disc-At-Once write mode, not Track-At-Once. Eugene developed and tested with Nero's Disc-At-Once/96. One movie per CD-R is the classic case. A CDDAFS CD-R is small; if you want more media (or larger files) per disc, a DVD-Video disc holds far more. For libraries of media, a rewritable storage device such as USB or MX4SIO is far more convenient than juggling discs.

title: Disc & console compatibility
text: ⚠ Optical playback depends on your drive and how you boot Every PS2 optical drive is a little different, and older drives read burned media less reliably as they age. A stock console typically needs a boot method (such as a memory-card exploit) to launch SMS in the first place; solutions like a modchip or a disc-boot exploit (e.g. FreeDVDBoot) change what the console will boot directly from a disc. title: Disc-related settings
text: SMS's Device settings include a couple of options that affect the optical drive: Option What it does Disable CD/DVD Turns off SMS's automatic CD/DVD detection, so SMS leaves the optical drive alone. Handy if probing the drive is slow or you never use discs. CD/DVD speed Controls the optical read speed (low / medium / high). A lower speed can help a marginal drive read a burned disc; a higher speed is faster when your media and drive are healthy. SMS also stops the disc spinning while a movie is paused or while you scroll the file list, and stops the drive at startup — small touches that keep the drive quieter and cooler. text: If your PS2 is connected to a receiver over its S/PDIF optical output, SMS can pass compressed Dolby Digital (AC3) and DTS audio through to that receiver rather than decoding it on the console — useful for films with surround soundtracks played from disc. This is unrelated to CD burning; it is just what SMS can do with a film's audio once it is playing.

title: Network Setup
text: Set up SMS networking for SMB shares or the UDPFS network drive: wired Ethernet, on-screen static IP configuration, server setup, protocol differences and the one-network-stack-per-boot rule.

title: Requirements
text: A fat PS2 with a Network Adapter , or a slim PS2 with built-in Ethernet. A wired Ethernet connection to the same LAN as the server PC. The PS2 has no built-in Wi-Fi. For SMB: a Windows, Samba or NAS host offering an SMB1/CIFS share. For UDPFS: PS2-Servers running its UDPFSD folder server.

title: Set the PS2's static IP on-screen
text: Open Device settings → Network settings → Edit IPCONFIG.DAT . Enter the PS2's own IP address, network mask and gateway one octet at a time, then choose Save/Update IPCONFIG.DAT . With a memory card present SMS writes mc0:/SYS-CONF/IPCONFIG.DAT , the same place the PS2 browser and other software expect it. With no memory card fitted it writes IPCONFIG.DAT beside SMS.ELF instead, and reads it back from there on the next boot — so a console with no card can still be given an address. UDPFS requires a valid static PS2 IP; SMB uses the same network configuration.

title: Choose an address
text: Give the PS2 an unused static address on the same subnet as the server, such as 192.168.1.20 when the PC is 192.168.1.10 .

title: Enter mask and gateway
text: For a typical home LAN the mask is 255.255.255.0 ; use your router's address as the gateway. Match your actual network.

title: Save
text: Choose Save/Update IPCONFIG.DAT . With a memory card fitted the file goes to the card, where the PS2 browser and other titles expect it; with no card fitted SMS writes it beside the ELF instead, and reads it back from there next boot — so a card-less console can still be networked.

title: Choosing a network mode
text: SMS can use the network in three different ways, and the console can only do one of them per boot . They all drive the same single network adapter, and an IOP module cannot be unloaded once it has claimed it — so the choice is settled the moment one starts. Because of that, the three autostart entries in Device settings behave as one setting rather than three switches: Mode What it is for Autostart HOST host: access from a PC running ps2client — mainly a development convenience. Autostart SMB A Windows / Samba / NAS file share. See SMB . Autostart UDPFS A folder served over UDP from a PC. See UDPFS below. Turning one on turns the other two off automatically. Selecting the one that is already

title: SMB network shares
text: The SMB browser stores a server address, share, user, password, client name and port. Add or edit the server under Device settings → Network settings → SMB server… using the on-screen keyboard; see SMB Network for the complete field reference. Start it with Start SMB support , or set Autostart SMB to have it come up on every boot. ⚠ SMB1 is required SMS speaks SMB1/CIFS. Modern Windows disables SMB1 by default, so a Samba/NAS configuration that permits SMB1 is usually safer than enabling an obsolete protocol broadly on a general-purpose PC. Keep this service on a trusted LAN.

title: UDPFS network drive
text: UDPFS serves a real PC directory over the UDPFS/UDPRDMA protocol. It is a file-level service: the folder mounts directly as udpfs: . It is not UDPBD, does not require a disk image, and does not appear as massN: .

title: Configure the PS2 IP
text: Complete the static-IP steps above and save IPCONFIG.DAT .

title: Serve the folder

title: Start the drive

When discovery succeeds, browse the udpfs: device like any other source. ✓ Hardware-confirmed in this fork Booting SMS from UDPFS, browsing and playing media from the served folder, and exiting playback cleanly have all been confirmed on real PS2 hardware.

When a desktop skin is set and loads successfully, its picture is stretched to fill the screen and replaces the default background ; if no skin is set (or a skin file fails to load), SMS falls back to its built-in desktop. ℹ A note on .mbf files Alo

title: Applying a skin
text: SMS looks for skin files in a Skins folder, and the location depends on how SMS was started:

title: Booted with a memory card
text: SMS looks on the memory card, under mc0:/SMS/Skins/ . A desktop skin named MyTheme is loaded from mc0:/SMS/Skins/MyTheme.smi .

title: Booted from another device (this fork)
text: If SMS was launched from USB, HDD or another device and reads its settings there, it also looks for skins in a Skins folder next to the SMS program on that boot device — so a memory-card-less setup can still carry its own skins. This matches the way this fork saves configuration to the boot device. See Settings Reference .

title: Select the skin, then save
text: Put the .smi file in the appropriate Skins folder, choose it from the on-screen menu, and save your settings so it is remembered. On the next redraw the desktop background changes to your skin. ⚠ If a skin doesn't appear Make sure the file has the exact .smi extension and sits directly in the Skins folder SMS is looking in (memory card or boot device, per above), and that the name you selected matches the file name. If a skin file can't be read or isn't a valid IPU image, SMS quietly falls back to its built-in desktop rather than showing an error — so a missing background usually means a wrong path, name or file format.

title: Making a skin
text: Because .smi is an IPU-encoded image and not a plain PNG or JPEG, you don't just rename a picture — the image has to be converted into the IPU format with a converter tool first. The workflow, conceptually, is:

title: Start from a full-screen image
text: Design your wallpaper at a normal screen resolution. SMS stretches the skin to fill the display, so a 4:3 image sized for standard-definition output gives the most predictable result.

title: Convert it to .smi
text: Run the image through an IPU converter to produce the .smi file. This is the step that turns an ordinary picture into something SMS's IPU decoder can load.

title: Drop it in Skins and select it
text: Copy the finished .smi into the Skins folder as in Applying a skin , pick it on-screen, and save. Why isn't a skin just a PNG or JPEG? The desktop skin loads through the PS2's IPU hardware, which decodes a specific image format rather than PNG/JPEG. Converting your picture to .smi up front means SMS can load and display the background quickly using the same hardware path it uses for video, without doing a general-purpose image decode every time it draws the desktop. The device and file icons in this fork are handled by a separate artwork pipeline and are built into the program, so they aren't part of the .smi skin.

title: Media Converter
text: SMS Media Converter: a desktop app that converts video and audio into formats SMS plays on a PS2. Presets, multi-pass encoding, keyframe interval, and Windows 10/11, Windows 7 and Linux builds.

title: Why convert at all
text: The PS2 decodes a specific and quite old set of formats, and most files downloaded today use none of them. In particular H.264 will never play — the console's video hardware handles MPEG‑1 and MPEG‑2 only, and everything else has to be decoded in software on a 294 MHz CPU. Converting is not a workaround; it is how a modern file gets onto this machine at all. Every output option the app offers is one SMS is known to handle. That is why the list is short: it is not a general-purpose encoder with a PS2 mode, it only makes files that work.

title: Presets
text: Each preset says what it is for and what it costs. If you are unsure, the first one is the right answer.

title: Video

MPEG‑2 (.mpg) Use if the Xvid preset stutters. The PS2's IPU chip decodes MPEG‑2 in hardware , so the CPU barely works and playback is the smoothest available. The trade is noticeably larger files. Roughly 4× the size of an MP3. Ogg Vorbis Slightly better quality than MP3 at the same size, and patent‑free. title: Multi-pass encoding
text: Encodes the video twice: the first run measures the material, the second spends the bitrate where it is actually needed. It matters more here than in a general‑purpose converter, because these presets aim at a fixed bitrate and a single pass has to guess how to spend it while still reading the file — so it commonly overshoots. Measured on a test clip asking for 800 kbps, one pass produced 959 and two produced 838. On a PS2 an overshoot is not merely a larger file: it is dropped frames over USB or a network share. The cost is roughly double the conversion time. The pass count is fixed at 2 . That is a limitation of FFmpeg, not of the format — MPEG‑4 Part 2 itself supports more, and the commer

title: Keyframe interval
text: How often a complete, self‑contained frame is written; everything between keyframes is stored as differences. This is what decides how fast seeking feels : jumping to any point means decoding forward from the previous keyframe, so a long interval can mean many seconds of work on a 294 MHz CPU before playback resumes. The default of 50 — about two seconds — sits at the knee of that curve. Raising it toward 300 saves only a few percent more file size but costs ten seconds or more on every jump. Keyframe interval is not the same as B‑frames. The two are routinely confused.
