The Windows 7 build is the same application compiled against Qt 5 and Python 3.8. It is not a reduced version; the presets and validation are identical.

title: Notes
text: MP4 files are written front‑loaded. The index is placed at the start of the file, so SMS can begin playing immediately instead of reading through the whole file first. Real Xvid is used when available. If your FFmpeg includes libxvid , the Xvid preset uses it rather than FFmpeg's built‑in encoder. Output is checked after conversion against the limits SMS actually has — resolution, stream count, packet size, and the 32‑bit file‑size ceiling.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Fix common SMS problems: unsupported or slow video, missing devices, SMB or UDPFS network failures, settings that do not save, and HD display issues.

title: A video stutters, drops frames, or won't play
text: SMS decodes video in software on the Emotion Engine and uses the PS2's IPU for colour conversion. That is a fixed budget — a file that is too demanding for the console will stutter no matter how fast your storage is. Work through these in order.

title: Confirm the format is supported
text: SMS plays a specific set of containers and codecs. If a file uses anything outside this list, it will fail to open or may play only its supported audio track. Supported video is AVI (DivX / Xvid / MPEG-4 Part 2), MP4 ( mp4v , MPEG-4 Part 2), and MPEG program streams (MPEG-1/2, .mpg / .mpeg ). H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, VP9, AV1 and WMV video are not supported — re-encode those to MPEG-4 Part 2 first. See Video Playback for the full format table.

title: Lower the bitrate and resolution
text: SMS rejects either video dimension above 1024 pixels , but passing that check does not guarantee real-time playback. Resolution, frame rate, B-frames, QPel/GMC, motion complexity, audio work, bitrate and storage speed all matter. Start from the confirmed 640×480, 30 fps, 1.5 Mbit/s MPEG-4 Part 2 profile and reduce resolution, frame rate or bitrate if needed. If the same file plays from USB but stutters over the network or from MX4SIO, storage throughput or fragmentation is the likely difference.

title: Rule out a damaged or fragmented file
text: A partial download, a bad burn, or a heavily fragmented file can cause hitching or a mid-file stop. Re-copy the file to the device (ideally to a freshly formatted or defragmented card/drive), or re-download it, and try again. A file that plays cleanly on a PC but stalls on the PS2 is the classic sign of a marginal encode or a bad copy.

title: Check the encode features
text: Interlaced MPEG-4 and MPEG-2 decode paths exist, but the current hardware fixture baseline is progressive. B-frames, QPel, GMC and interlacing can add work or expose compatibility differences. If a supported file is marginal, re-encode it progressive with no B-frames using the known-good command on the Video Playback page. ⚠ Audio-only files that won't play The same "is it a supported format" rule applies to audio. SMS handles MP3, AAC, AC3, FLAC, OGG Vorbis and WMA . A file with an unusual codec inside a familiar-looking container (for example a lossless track the decoder doesn't recognise) can fail to open — re-encode to plain MP3 to confirm the file, then work back from there.

title: A storage device doesn't appear
text: If a device you plugged in isn't showing in the top-row device menu, it's almost always one of three things: it isn't started, it isn't formatted the way SMS expects, or it's blocked by a mutual exclusion.

title: Start the device (or turn on its Autostart)
text: On a clean install nothing auto-starts — this is by design (see below). Open the settings menu and either flip on that device's Autostart toggle (Autostart USB, Autostart MX4SIO, Autostart HDD APA, Autostart HDD flip on that device's Autostart toggle (Autostart USB, Autostart i.LINK, Autostart MX4SIO, Autostart MMCE, Autostart HDD APA, Autostart HDD BDM for ATA/exFAT, then the three mutually exclusive network rows — Autostart HOST ( ps2dev ) , Autostart SMB and Autostart UDPFS , where picking one clears the other two), or use the matching Start … item that appears when a device isn't running yet. Starting it on demand does not need a reboot.

title: Check the filesystem format
text: BDM mass devices (USB, MX4SIO, ATA/exFAT) expect a FAT32 or exFAT filesystem. A drive formatted NTFS, HFS+ or ext4 will not mount. Re-format the card or drive as FAT32 (or exFAT for large volumes) and copy your media back. The internal-HDD APA/PFS path is different — that uses a PlayStation 2 PFS partition rather than a PC filesystem; see Internal HDD .

title: Rule out a mutual exclusion
text: Three resource pairs cannot both be active in one boot: MX4SIO and MMCE both use the SIO2 / memory-card-slot bus. If one is running, the other won't appear — turn off the one you don't need. The internal HDD APA/PFS path and the ATA/exFAT (BDM) path both own the internal ATA bus. Whichever starts first owns it; pick one. SMB/host and UDPFS load different stacks for the single Ethernet controller. Reboot, then start only the network path you intend to use. ℹ How devices are named BDM mass devices (USB, MX4SIO, ATA/exFAT, i.LINK) all share the massN: namespace, with N counting up from 0. MMCE devices are mmce0: / mmce1: . The internal APA/PFS HDD is hdd0: , and the UDPFS folder is udpfs: . If

title: An SMB share won't connect
text: SMS speaks the older SMB1 / CIFS network-share protocol. By far the most common reason a share won't connect is that the server no longer accepts SMB1. ✖ Top cause: SMB1 is disabled on the server Modern Windows and Samba ship with SMB1 turned off by default for security. SMS needs it enabled to connect. This is a server-side setting, not something SMS can work around from the PS2. How do I re-enable SMB1 on the server? On Windows: open Turn Windows features on or off and enable SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support (specifically the client/server sub-features), then reboot. Be aware SMB1 is legacy and considered insecure — only enable it on a trusted local network, and consider a dedicated share

title: Verify the address, share name and credentials
text: Once SMB1 is on, re-check the server's IP address, the exact share name, and the username/password — all entered on-screen with the built-in keyboard (see Network Setup ). A typo in any of these looks identical to "server refused". Case can matter for share names and usernames.

title: Check the PS2's own network settings
text: Make sure the PS2 has a valid static IP on the same subnet as the server, saved through Device settings → Network settings → Edit IPCONFIG.DAT , and that the network device is started. If the console can't reach the network at all, no share will connect.

title: Check firewalls and the server's file sharing
text: A firewall on the server (or router) can block the PS2's connection even with everything else correct. Confirm file sharing is enabled on the server and that its firewall allows connections from the PS2's IP on your local network. ⚠ SMB1 is a legacy protocol The SMB client in SMS is the legacy SMB1 stack, and modernising it to SMB2 is separate work beyond this build. If you can't or won't enable SMB1 on your server, use the UDPFS network drive or a directly-attached device instead.

title: The UDPFS network drive won't appear
text: Save the PS2's own static IP through Edit IPCONFIG.DAT ; a NOIP error means this step is missing. Run PS2-Servers UDPFSD on a PC on the same LAN, select the folder to serve, and keep Modulo mode off . Allow UDP port 0xF5F6 (62966) through the PC firewall on the trusted LAN. If SMB/host was already started, reboot before choosing Start UDPFS network drive . The two stacks cannot share the NIC in one boot.

title: Settings don't persist across reboots
text: If your Autostart toggles, network details or playback preferences reset every time you power on, the config isn't being saved — or isn't being found on the next boot.

title: Insert a memory card (or understand where config goes)
text: By default SMS saves its configuration to the memory card at mc0:/SMS/SMS.cfg . No memory card in slot 1 means nowhere to write — so settings can't persist. Insert a memory card and save again.

title: This fork can save to the boot device instead
text: If SMS was booted from another device (USB, HDD…) and there's no memory card, this fork saves the config next to the SMS ELF on that boot device instead. So a memory-card-less setup can still keep its settings — as long as the boot device is writable and present at each boot.

title: Save after changing settings
text: Make your changes, then save through the settings menu so they're written out. If a setting only ever holds for the current session, it wasn't committed to storage. ℹ Resetting to a clean state Deleting the config file returns SMS to clean defaults — which means nothing auto-starts and every Autostart toggle is off. If SMS is misbehaving after a lot of tweaking, clearing the config is a reliable way to get back to a known-good baseline; you then turn back on only the devices you use.

title: Nothing starts up on the first boot
text: ℹ This is by design On a clean install, no device auto-starts . SMS boots to the desktop with the device menu waiting, and you enable what you need. This is deliberate — it avoids forcing a device (such as an internal HDD) that you may not have, and it keeps the first boot fast and predictable. To bring a device online, either turn on its Autostart toggle in settings (so it comes up automatically on future boots) or use the matching Start <device> now item to start it immediately without rebooting. Once you save your settings, your chosen devices will auto-start from then on. This is expected behaviour, not a fault.

title: The screen looks corrupted in HD video modes
text: ⚠ Known issue in HD output modes In the two high-definition modes (720p and 1080i) SMS does not draw the desktop wallpaper at all — it paints a plain gradient background instead. This is deliberate: the HD framebuffer leaves no room in VRAM for the full-screen artwork, and forcing it there used to comb the text and leave black bars. Everything else works normally; if you want the artwork, use a standard-definition mode (480i/480p/576p), all of which are unaffected. HD modes use a much larger framebuffer than standard definition, which leaves little room for the full-screen desktop artwork; the result can be a corrupted or garbled background on the desktop. title: Reporting a freeze
text: If SMS stops responding during startup and a power cycle is the only way out, there is a build that can tell us exactly where it stopped. Simple-Media-System-DIAG.elf , published alongside every release, is the same code with one addition: before each step of startup it prints a short code such as E44 in the status bar, naming the step it is about to perform. If that step never finishes, the code stays on screen . So the last code visible is the thing that hung. It needs no network and no memory card — the codes are drawn directly by the console's graphics hardware, so they still appear when almost nothing else is working. That is the whole point: it reports faults that a log file could not,

title: How to use it
text: Fix common SMS problems: unsupported or slow video, missing devices, SMB or UDPFS network failures, settings that do not save, and HD display issues.

title: Run it
text: Boot Simple-Media-System-DIAG.elf the same way you boot the normal ELF.

title: Watch the status bar
text: Codes appear at the bottom of the screen as startup progresses. On a healthy console they flick past quickly and you end up at the file browser.

title: Note where it stops
text: If it freezes, write down or photograph the last code shown. A recording is even better — it captures the order they appeared in.

title: Report it
text: Open an issue with that code, your console model, and what was connected. One code usually identifies the exact call. Use the standard ELF for normal playback — the diagnostic build is not faster or better, it simply talks more.

title: Building from Source
text: How to build SMS from source: the pinned ps2dev/ps2dev:v1.0 Docker toolchain, running make to produce bin/SMS.elf, the embedded IOP driver modules, the patched MX4SIO driver, and continuous integration.

title: Prerequisites
text: The build uses the pinned ps2dev toolchain image, so the only thing you need on your machine is Docker and a checkout of the source tree. Everything else — the EE compiler, the IOP compiler, the PS2SDK headers and libraries, bin2c , and so on — comes from inside the container. Docker installed and running (Docker Desktop on Windows/macOS, or the Docker engine on Linux). A clone of the SMS source tree (this repository), including its committed irx/ and images/ assets. Enough disk to pull the toolchain image the first time you run it.

title: The pinned toolchain image
text: SMS builds against a single, version-pinned toolchain image: ps2dev/ps2dev:v1.0 . This is the public PS2 homebrew toolchain (its EE compiler is ee-gcc 3.2.3 ). Pinning to a specific tag matters — it is what lets the build be reproducible: the project's CI produces a byte-identical ELF from the same source on this exact image. Do not substitute a "latest" tag; use v1.0 . ⚠ Why only the build runs in the container The ps2dev/ps2dev:v1.0 image is built on an older Alpine (musl) base. That base is fine for compiling, but modern GitHub Actions steps (checkout, artifact upload) run JavaScript on a Node runtime that this old musl can't load. So on CI the checkout happens on the host and only the ma

title: Building the EE app
text: From the root of the source tree, run the toolchain container with the repo mounted and invoke make . The image is minimal, so the command also installs the small build-base package set it needs before building: docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src -w /src ps2dev/ps2dev:v1.0 \ sh -c 'apk add --no-cache build-base && make all' That single command compiles every EE source file, embeds the IOP driver modules and the artwork, links the program, and strips it. The output is: bin/SMS.elf

title: Mount the repo into the container
text: -v "$PWD":/src -w /src maps your current directory (the repo root) to /src inside the container and makes it the working directory, so the build writes bin/SMS.elf straight back onto your host filesystem. --rm discards the container when it exits.

title: Install the build-base and run make
text: apk add --no-cache build-base pulls in the host-side build tools the make run needs; then make all does the actual compile and link. On CI the same step also adds git and zip for packaging, but a plain local build only needs build-base .

title: Collect the ELF
text: When make finishes, the finished program is at bin/SMS.elf . That is the file you copy to a device and boot — see Install & First Boot . The build defaults to the full-device configuration ( BDM ?= 1 in the Makefile), which enables the BDM storage stack and the extra devices. That is the configuration this documentation describes, and the one you want. What if I'm on Windows and $PWD isn't expanded? $PWD is a shell variable that expands to the current directory in a POSIX shell (bash, Git Bash, WSL, macOS/Linux terminals). In PowerShell use ${PWD} , and in cmd.exe use %cd% . The rest of the command is identical. The important part is that the repo root is bind-mounted to /src and make all ru

title: Embedded IOP driver modules
text: SMS runs its storage and I/O drivers on the PS2's IOP (I/O Processor) as .irx modules. Rather than load these off a device at runtime, SMS embeds them into the ELF at build time and loads them from memory as it boots. That is what makes SMS self-contained — the single bin/SMS.elf carries every driver it needs. The Makefile lists the module set that gets linked in (the IOP_OBJS group, gated behind BDM=1 ). In this fork that set is: Module Role iomanx Extended I/O manager — the modern file-I/O core the device layers sit on filexio EE↔IOP file-I/O bridge (the fileXio API SMS uses for BDM devices) bdm Block Device Manager — the common layer all massN: devices share bdmfs_fatfs FAT / exFAT filesy

title: The patched MX4SIO driver
text: The headline feature of this fork — reliable MX4SIO playback — depends on a hardened version of the mx4sio_bd block-device driver. That driver is not the stock one: it is rebuilt from the PS2SDK source with reliability hardening so playback stays robust under the demands a continuously-streaming media player puts on the console. So that the embedded binary is reproducible and reviewable, the patch is kept in the repo alongside the built module: patches/mx4sio_bd-sms.patch — the source patch, applied to PS2SDK's iop/sio/mx4sio_bd/ . irx/mx4sio_bd.irx — the resulting hardened module (committed compressed, like the others), which the EE app embeds. title: Continuous integration
text: A GitHub Actions workflow ( .github/workflows/compilation.yml ) builds SMS on every push (and on pull requests and version tags). It checks the tree out on the host, then runs the same docker run … ps2dev/ps2dev:v1.0 … make all build inside the pinned container — the identical command you run locally — and packages the resulting bin/SMS.elf . text: Install Docker ; no local toolchain needed. Build with docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/src -w /src ps2dev/ps2dev:v1.0 sh -c 'apk add --no-cache build-base && make all' . Output is bin/SMS.elf (default full-device / BDM=1 build). All IOP driver modules are embedded into the ELF from the committed, XZ-compressed irx/ .
